title: California Permit Test Day: What Happens at the DMV
description: The California learner's permit visit in order: online application, documents and fee, the 4:30 p.m. test cutoff, vision check, the 80% test, and retakes.
intro: Most people who prepare for the California permit test spend all their time on road rules and almost none on the visit itself. Yet a missing document, a late arrival, or a parent who stayed home can end the day before the test even starts. This guide walks through one permit visit in the order the California DMV describes it, from the online application to what the permit allows once you pass. Everything here comes from DMV pages and the California Driver's Handbook (June 2025 edition) checked on November 5, 2026. Rules and fees can change, so take a quick look at the DMV site the week of your visit.

sections.heading: Step one happens at home: the online application
sections.body:
The DMV asks you to start the Driver's License or ID Card Application online, then finish it in person. Teens getting a learner's permit also start here.

- You need a MyDMV account. The DMV uses two-factor sign-in, so have an email address and a phone that can get a call or text.
- Keep your Social Security number at hand. The DMV says the law requires it if you have one.
- The DMV estimates about 9 minutes to fill out the form. The page times out after 15 minutes, but you can log back in and finish later. A saved application is kept for up to a year.
- The form is offered in 10 languages, including Spanish, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, and Tagalog.
- When you submit, you get a confirmation number by email. The office worker can use it to pull up your application, so keep that email.

**Under 18:** you need your own MyDMV account, and your parent or guardian needs a separate one to approve your application. After they approve, the system prompts you to book an appointment and upload your documents.

sections.heading: What to carry to the office
sections.body:
Uploading documents online saves time, but the DMV says to bring them with you anyway. Put these in one folder the night before:

1. **Proof of identity**, such as a valid passport or birth certificate. The DMV wants an original or a certified copy, and your current full name must match it. If your name has changed, bring the document that shows the change.
2. **Two proofs of California residency**, such as a utility bill or bank statement. The handbook asks for two, with some exceptions, and a REAL ID requires two.
3. **Your Social Security number.**
4. **Payment for the application fee.** The DMV fee table lists $46 for an original Class C license application. The fee is non-refundable, and the application and fee are good for 12 months.
5. **Under 18 only:** a certificate showing you completed driver education, or that you are enrolled in an approved combined driver education and training program. A parent or guardian must also come with you to sign. If both parents share joint custody, the handbook says both must sign.

sections.heading: At the office: the steps in order, and the 4:30 cutoff
sections.body:
The DMV lists the office part of the permit visit in this order: a technician reviews your documents, you pay the fee, you take a vision exam, you have your photo taken, and then you take the knowledge test.

**Watch the clock.** DMV pages say knowledge tests are not given after 4:30 p.m. and must be started before then, to leave enough time to finish. The checks before the test take time too, so a morning slot is the safe choice.

**The vision exam.** If you wear glasses or contact lenses for the vision exam, your license will carry a corrective lenses restriction. If you do not pass, the DMV will ask you to have an eye doctor fill out a Report of Vision Examination (form DL 62). That can delay your permit, so if you have not had an eye exam in a while, consider getting one before your visit.

sections.heading: Inside the knowledge test
sections.body:
The test is multiple choice, and every question comes from the California Driver's Handbook. Here is how the DMV describes it:

- Each question has three answers. One is correct, and the other two are either plainly wrong or do not fit the question. The DMV says there are no trick questions, so do not overthink.
- The passing score is 80 percent.
- You may not use any testing aids, including the handbook or a cell phone. Expect to put your phone away.
- If you miss a question, the office worker can tell you the handbook page where the right answer is.

That last point is worth using. If you pass but missed a few questions, ask for those page numbers and write them down. Those pages are the gaps you still need to fill before you start driving.

sections.heading: If you do not pass the first time
sections.body:
One application gives you **three attempts** at the knowledge test. If you fail the same test three times, your application is no longer valid and you have to reapply.

If you are under 18, the handbook says you must wait seven days to retake a failed knowledge test, not counting the day you failed. For example, if you fail on a Monday, the earliest retake is the Tuesday of the next week.

Use the waiting days well. Write down the handbook pages for the questions you missed, read those pages first, and then practice only the topic each one came from. Going back over the whole handbook again is slower and leaves the same weak spots.

sections.heading: After you pass: what the permit lets you do
sections.body:
Passing the knowledge test gets you a permit to practice, not a license to drive alone.

- **18 or older:** you get an instruction permit. You may drive only with a California-licensed driver who is at least 18 and sits close enough to take control of the car.
- **Under 18:** you get a provisional instruction permit, and you must wait to use it until you start behind-the-wheel training with an instructor, who validates the permit. Your practice driver must be at least 25.
- **Before the drive test (under 18):** hold the permit for at least six months, finish 6 hours of professional driver training, and log 50 hours of practice with a licensed adult 25 or older. At least 10 of those hours must be at night.

The DMV says permits are good for up to one year from the application date. If you are under 18 and your application runs out before your six months are up, you reapply at an office, and the time you already held the permit still counts. Bring both the expired and the new permit to the drive test.

sections.heading: Your plan for the week before the visit
sections.body:
1. **Seven days out:** finish the online application, and make sure a parent has approved it if you are under 18. Book the earliest appointment you can get.
2. **Five days out:** gather your identity document, two residency documents, and, if under 18, the driver education certificate. Check that the name on each one matches your application.
3. **Every day this week:** do one short practice set on this site, rotating through the five topics: signs and signals, right of way, speed and parking, safe driving, and alcohol and phone laws. On the DMV test, 80 percent is the bar, so keep practicing until you clear it with some room to spare.
4. **Two days out:** take one full mock exam here, and also try the free sample tests on the DMV website.
5. **The day before:** put every document and the confirmation email in one folder, and plan to arrive well before 4:30 p.m.

faq.question: Can I take the California permit knowledge test online?
faq.answer: The handbook says your testing options appear once you complete your application online, so check there first. One thing is clear: the DMV's eLearning course replaces the knowledge test only for people renewing a regular Class C license. Original applicants do not qualify for it.

faq.question: I'm 17 and a half. Do I still need driver education to get a permit?
faq.answer: No. The DMV says applicants older than 17½ but under 18 can get an instruction permit without the driver education and training certificates. However, you cannot take the drive test until you turn 18.

faq.question: Does my parent have to come to the DMV with me?
faq.answer: Yes, if you are under 18. The DMV's Teen Driver Roadmap says a parent or guardian needs to be with you at the appointment, and the handbook says both parents must sign if they share joint custody. By signing, they also accept financial responsibility for your driving.
